title: Former Bobby G’s employees and contractors point to pattern of missed payments and poor communication - Berkeleyside
content: Nonprofit news. Free for all, funded by readers. UC Berkeley alum Calvin Miller was first drawn to Bobby G’s Pizzeria for its New York-style pizza and wide selection of draught beers. Before long, Bobby G’s became his neighborhood haunt for Sunday night NFL games, wings, and the occasional Wednesday trivia night, which was popular among college students. In May 2025, the opportunity arose to work at Bobby G’s as a server; Miller said that it felt like an easy decision. He signed some brief paperwork and joined the front-of-house staff the next day. It was shortly after getting his first paycheck that the problems started. “From that moment on, everything went downhill,” Miller said in an interview with Nosh, describing a pattern of delayed paychecks and poor communication about the late payments from restaurant owners Gurpreet Kaur and Gurmukh “Jay” Bansel Singh. Miller is not the only former employee of Bobby G’s to allege similar experiences. In March, the restaurant’s former social media coordinator, Jennifer Baquing, filed a lawsuit in the Alameda County Superior Court alleging wage violations, failure to reimburse business expenses and employee misclassification, among other complaints. Shortly afterwards, in April 2026, Bobby G’s closed indefinitely. Baquing named Game & Co, Inc – the corporate parent of Bobby G’s Pizzeria – and its shareholders, Singh and Kaur, as defendants. According to the complaint, Kaur and Singh “systematically” underpaid and withheld wages during her time of employment before terminating her year-long employment contract in late December 2025, well ahead of its Oct. 16, 2026 expiration date — a breach of her signed contract that insured compensation for early termination without proper notice or cause. Baquing and her attorney, Alexei Kuchinsky, declined to comment at this time. Over about 10 weeks from the end of May through July, East Bay Nosh tried to reach Kaur for comment via cellphone, the restaurant’s landline, email and a LinkedIn message, but he did not respond. On July 23, Bansel Singh sent Nosh a text message and email asking for Nosh to contact him. However, despite numerous follow-up attempts by us on that day, and leading up to publication of this report, including phone calls, text and email messages, Singh has not been in touch again. East Bay Nosh spoke with former employees, contractors and vendors who worked at or with Bobby G’s while it was run by Kaur and Singh. Similar to Baquing and Miller, they described a pattern of missed or delayed payments and erratic communication from ownership. The restaurant at 2072 University Ave. remains dark, and a “Now Leasing” sign has been posted in the window by Raj Properties. Bobby G’s first opened in late December 2006 as a small pizzeria owned by Berkeley native Robert Gaustad. Prior to Bobby G’s, Gaustad had lived in over 33 cities –working across film, food, and tech – before he returned home to pursue his dream of opening a restaurant. Gaustad and his partner, Heather Kratt, purchased the Indian-pizza fusion restaurant for sale on 2072 University Ave. in October 2006 and quickly got to work to bring their vision to life. “For me, if I was going to be in a restaurant that I own and work seven days a week in, for up to 12 hours a day, I wanted it to have the things that I like: sports, beer, and music,” said Gaustad who is also a blues harmonica player. With time, the result was a bustling sports bar that sold 13 beers on tap and pizza made from Bay Area-sourced ingredients like Giusto’s flour. “If your ingredients are poor, you can’t fix that, but we had good ingredients, good pizza and good chefs like Keith [McNabb],” Gaustad said. The space also offered an abundance of tabletop seating as well as cozy sofas pushed against the walls adorned with sports jerseys and framed photos of musicians. “It was Berkeley’s living room,” Berkeley photojournalist Aaron Rosenblatt told East Bay Nosh while scrolling through the photos he took of Bobby G’s throughout the last decade. “Anyone could sit as long as they didn’t cause trouble.” As shown by Rosenblatt’s photos, the restaurant went on to see Bogart, the neighborhood husky, regularly beg at the bar for chicken scraps, a crowd of locals raise a glass to chef McNabb — called “the greatest guy and punkrocker” by Gaustad after he passed away from cancer in 2017 — and the construction of an outdoors seating parklet, at no cost, by the Bobby G’s regular Tibor Lageman in 2020. Across those years, Bobby G’s weekly bluegrass jams and trivia nights continued to attract large crowds, as did the annual release of the limited-edition Pliny the Younger beer from the Russian Brewing Company. On the Pliny release day at Bobby G’s, a heavily congested line would form down University Avenue and around Citibank, with people hailing from across the East Bay. During one year’s release, recalled by Gaustad, the keg ran dry in only 47 minutes. “I did the 10-ounce pours, lined them up, over and over, and suddenly it was over,” much to the chagrin of those who remained in line for the coveted beer. In 2016, Gaustad sold Bobby G’s to the brothers Karan and Randeep Rekhi after a dispute with the restaurant’s landlord, Raj Properties, which did not respond to multiple requests for comment. While the neighborhood haunt survived multiple ownership changes and the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic, trouble emerged after the 2024 handoff to Kaur and Singh, according to multiple Bobby G’s contractors and employees. In February 2025, the owner of Trivia CA, Chris O’Brien — who is also the partner of Jennifer Baquing, who filed the lawsuit — received a direct message on Instagram from the former Bobby G’s trivia hosts who warned him of delayed payments from Kaur and Singh. O’Brien, who was considering a job offer from Bobby G’s at the time, said he raised the issue of delayed payments during his first meeting with management on March 19, 2025. Management allegedly assured him: “There’s not going to be any problem paying you.” For the first few months, O’Brien said that his payments arrived mostly on time. Trivia nights boomed under O’Brien’s watch with the average number of players increasing from 40 to 80, and sometimes 120 on the most crowded nights. Despite the buzz, O’Brien said his payments began to habitually fall behind schedule, and he regularly had to remind ownership to send him his fees. East Bay Nosh reviewed screenshots of text messages between Singh and O’Brien, supplied to us by O’Brien, that corroborated the pattern of delayed payments and subsequent excuses from ownership. O’Brien departed in January 2026 due to the financial strain and stress. While he received the money owed to him in the end, others did not have the same experience. Berkeley resident Ian Powell, a professional brewer, alleges that Kaur and Singh contracted him to design and rebuild a cold box with a direct draw system (a refrigerated cabinet for dispensing beer on tap) for the restaurant in July 2024. According to Powell, all parties agreed that he would receive $8,000 as outlined by the estimate. Powell described the relationship as initially positive, recalling comments from Singh like, “Man, my dude, I can’t wait to work with you.” But the arrangement later deteriorated. Powell said that on multiple occasions Kaur and Singh failed to show up to let him into the restaurant to continue his work, leaving him and his business partners stranded while calls went unanswered. Powell said the final blow came when Kaur paid only $1,000 despite the completed designs and contractor coordination. Powell was then unable to complete the job. “They frosted me out of the place and made it clear they didn’t have the money to pay,” Powell said. Miller, the former server, said that, in addition to consistently late payments and bounced checks, the work environment was unhealthy in other ways. For example, employees were not given regular breaks as mandated by California Labor Law, and the owners would dodge their calls and communications regsrding the payments. Two former Bobby G’s employees who did not wish to speak on the record corroborated Miller’s account of late payments and poor communication from management. “It got to a point where I said, I won’t come to work until I’m paid,” Miller said. He eventually gave his final warning to ownership that he would quit if he didn’t receive his next payment on time. Miller said his next payment was delayed by a week, forcing him to borrow money from a roommate for his graduation cap and gown. He quit in November 2025. Baquing was hired to be the social media manager for Bobby G’s in April 2025. The lawsuit claims that although Baquing was working as an employee, ownership misclassified her as a contractor in order to “evade their obligations under California wage-and-hour laws.” The lawsuit also claims Baquing was routinely paid “days or weeks late,” and multiple checks issued to her were returned for insufficient funds, while also alleging Kaur and Singh improperly commingled Game & Co Inc’s funds with their own funds and diverted assets from the business to themselves. Baquing signed a new one-year contract also signed by Kaur that was to run from Oct. 16, 2025 to Oct. 16, 2026 and included, among several provisions, stipulations on payment, pay frequency, and an early termination fee. Then, the lawsuit claims, on Dec. 18, 2025, Kaur and Singh “unilaterally terminated [Baquing] without cause, without notice, and without paying the contractually obligated early termination compensation,” amounting to $90,600. While the lawsuit filed by Baquing makes its way through court, Bobby G’s now sits empty, waiting for a new tenant. An initial case management hearing is scheduled for Oct. 6, 2026. The news of its closure saddened Gaustad, who called the restaurant his “baby.” “We worked hard to build that place and clientele, and we made a lot of lifelong friends doing it,” he said. Gaustad is now retired in Petaluma but had looked forward to visiting Bobby G’s this December for what would have been the pizzeria’s 20th anniversary. Gaustad said that he and Singh had even texted briefly about throwing a celebration to commemorate two decades of Bobby G’s history. “I wish it had lasted longer and I think it would have, if people had kept the quality and kept doing the right thing,” said Gaustad. title: Drake Makes Shocking Appearance At Karol G's Concert In Toronto - iHeart
content: Drake surprised thousands of fans when he showed up to support Karol G during her tour stop in his hometown. The Grammy Award-winning singer made a stop at Rogers Stadium in Toronto on Tuesday night, July 29, to perform songs off her recent album Tropicoqueta and other bangers as part of her "Vijando Por El Mundo Tropitour." During the show, Drizzy appeared on the giant LED screens while he was in the crowd and flashed a huge grin to the people. He threw up the 6 as he danced to the music in his VIP section. Drake and Karol G have never collaborated before, but the two are rumored to have worked on a song together for Karol's upcoming album. It wouldn't be The Boy's first time dabbling in the Latin world. The Canadian rapper has joined forces with the likes of Bad Bunny, Romeo Santos, and, most recently, Chino Pacas. He first flexed his Spanish skills by crooning his verse alongside Romeo on their 2014 track "Odio," produced by Rico Love. Later, in 2018, Drake joined forces with El Conejo Malo on "MIA," where he rapped his verse in Spanish. The two reunited in 2023 for "Gently" off Drake's album For All The Dogs. He also has two songs with Chino Pacas, "Modo Capone" with Fuerza Regida and "Meet Your Padre" with PARTYNEXTDOOR. from their joint album $ome $exy $ongs 4 U. Karol G also has some crossover experience under her belt. Her most notable hip-hop collaboration to date is "Tusa" featuring Nicki Minaj. The Colombian singer has also worked with Migos, Snoop Dogg, Pitbull, EDM legend Tiesto, as well as singers Jessie Reyez and Kali Uchis. While her current tour supports her latest album, Karol G is actively preparing to deliver her next LP, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto. Look out for her new album arriving August 7. title: Attempted murder complaint filed against Rucsu GS Ammar, 8 others over RU library assault - tbsnews.net
content: An attempted murder complaint has been filed before a Rajshahi court against Rajshahi University Central Students' Union (Rucsu) General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar and eight others Rucsu and Islami Chhatra Shibir leaders over the assault on a student inside the university's central library. The complaint was filed yesterday (30 July) at the Cognisance Court of Rajshahi's Motihar Police Station by MS Asad Uz Zaman, father of injured student Mahmudul Hasan, according to court sources. The court directed the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) to investigate the allegations, according to the complainant's lawyer Hazrat Ali. Other accused are Rucsu Assistant General Secretary Salman Sabbir, Information and Research Secretary BM Nazmus Sakib, Deputy Information and Research Secretary Sifat Abu Saleh, Shahid Ziaur Rahman Hall GS Ariful Islam, Shahid Habibur Rahman Hall Vice-President Ahsan Ullah Farhan, Nawab Abdul Latif Hall GS Nurul Islam Shahid, Rajshahi University unit Chhatra Shibir Media and Publicity Secretary Mehedi Sajib, and Senate student representative Fahim Reza. The complaint also names 17 to 18 unidentified individuals. According to the complaint, between 12:30pm and 1pm on 27 July, a group of 19 to 20 people armed with iron rods, bamboo sticks and other weapons surrounded Mahmudul Hasan inside the university's central library and assaulted him with the intention of killing him. The complaint alleges that Ammar repeatedly struck the victim on the head and forehead with an iron rod, while the other accused also beat him with rods and bamboo sticks, causing serious injuries. It further claims that several attackers pinned him to the ground and attempted to suffocate him by pressing on his chest and neck. Even after volunteers and locals rescued him and placed him in an ambulance, the attackers allegedly dragged him out and assaulted him again. Lawyer Hazrat Ali said the court has asked the PBI to submit its investigation report within the stipulated time. The case stems from an incident on 27 July in which three students, including one accused of having links to the banned Chhatra League, were allegedly assaulted by Rucsu and Chhatra Shibir leaders and activists inside the university's central library following an earlier altercation at the proctor's office. On 29 July, a group of Rajshahi University students formed a human chain in front of the central library, demanding action against Rucsu and Chhatra Shibir leaders over the alleged assault. The protest, held under the banner of general students, was addressed by Rajshahi University Chhatra Dal President Sultan Ahmed Rahi, Organising Secretary Mahmudul Hasan Mithu and others. title: Watch Thieves Abandon a BMW R 1200 GS Theft — Possibly Because It Was Stuck in Gear - Yahoo Autos
content: Motorcycle thefts involving high-value machines have become increasingly common in the UK, but stealing one isn't always as simple as riding away. In some cases, thieves discover too late that operating certain motorcycles requires more than just confidence. That appeared to be the case when two men attempted to steal what appeared to be a BMW R 1200 GS. Despite their efforts, they were unable to get the motorcycle moving and were eventually forced to abandon the theft altogether. Although the owner avoided losing the motorcycle, the failed theft still left it damaged after one of the suspects dropped it and walked away without putting it back on its stand. While insurance may cover the repairs, the owner was at least fortunate to find the bike exactly where it had been parked. The incident was captured on video and shared on Instagram, giving viewers a close look at how the attempted theft unfolded. A video shared on Instagram by SpeedSquad showing two motorcycle-borne thieves attempting to steal a BMW R 1200 GS has gone viral, racking up more than 495,000 views in one day. The footage began with one suspect standing beside the motorcycle while the other climbed onto the GS and, with help from his accomplice, broke the handlebar lock within seconds. Their next challenge, however, was getting away on the bike, which retailed for well over $15,000 when new in the U.S. One of the suspects then tried to lift the heavily leaning adventure bike off its side stand, but it quickly became apparent that he was unfamiliar with handling a large motorcycle as he struggled to control its weight. After retracting the side stand, he attempted to push the BMW forward, but it refused to budge. One possible explanation is that the bike was left in gear rather than neutral, locking the rear wheel and preventing it from rolling. Another possibility is that the owner had fitted a front disc lock that remained in place. Two broken pieces visible on the ground near the front wheel suggest the thieves may have tried to force it open but failed to remove it completely. The suspect made several unsuccessful attempts to push the motorcycle before apparently realizing they were running out of time. Fearing they might be caught, the pair abandoned the theft and fled the scene. In frustration, the thief let the BMW crash onto its side instead of placing it back on its stand, leaving the owner with damage but, fortunately, not a stolen motorcycle. It is not known whether the suspects were ever identified or arrested, or whether the owner pursued legal action. Despite the damage, the owner still had his motorcycle at the end of the day. title: Why Mikaela Shiffrin Keeps Going: Curiosity, GS and Super-G - Ski Racing Media
content: Mikaela Shiffrin has collected enough victories, medals and crystal globes to fill several remarkable careers. Yet the most successful alpine ski racer in history says those numbers reveal little about why she continues. In her YouTube video, “Why Do You Keep Going? | My Honest Answer,” Shiffrin offers an unusually open account of her current thinking. The solo episode of her “What’s the Point?” series explores motivation, retirement, giant slalom, super-G and the demanding offseason hidden behind her public appearances. Her answer to the question surrounding the next stage of her career comes down to one word: curiosity. “I just want to learn what’s around the corner,” Shiffrin said. “And I want to see if the work that I do right now can impact what’s around the corner in a positive way.” At 31, Shiffrin understands why questions about retirement have become more valid. She also leaves little doubt about her immediate intentions. Shiffrin recited a career résumé that includes 110 World Cup victories, 168 World Cup podiums and 18 crystal globes. She also listed three Olympic gold medals and 15 world championship medals, including eight golds. Reading those achievements aloud made her uncomfortable. “It’s cool, but it’s hard to connect with it,” Shiffrin said. Her latest season added another extraordinary chapter. She won nine of 10 slaloms and secured the discipline title before the end of January. She also earned her sixth overall globe and returned to the top of the Olympic slalom podium. Still, statistics cannot recreate the sensation of solving a technical problem, finding speed in training or producing the turns she imagined during Olympic pressure. For Shiffrin, that connection remains more meaningful than any numerical milestone. “It’s always been about the turns,” she said. “That’s what I can feel.” Her Olympic slalom victory provided the clearest example. Shiffrin carried a substantial advantage into the second run but refused to ski protectively. “I skied my heart out,” Shiffrin said. “It was the best run of slalom that I’ve ever done on that stage.” She took the risk that her approach might not work. The reward came from skiing the turns she wanted in the sport’s biggest environment. The gold medal confirmed the result, but the skiing gave the moment its meaning. Shiffrin’s slalom dominance commanded the brightest spotlight, but her progress in giant slalom may have carried greater personal significance. While rebuilding after her November 2024 crash in Killington, Vermont, Shiffrin fell to 30th in the giant slalom World Cup Start List rankings. By the end of the 2025-26 season, she had climbed back into the top seven and ranked fourth. Shiffrin called that recovery “a monumental step” for herself and her team. Shiffrin believes the level of women’s giant slalom has risen since she won her last discipline globe. She described the current field as more powerful and faster, with athletes performing at an exceptionally high level. Rather than finding that development discouraging, she finds it exciting. “I don’t know if I can consistently win GSs or win at all,” she said. “There were moments this past season where I felt like that level was within reach.” At other times, she questioned whether she could reach it. Shiffrin returned to several super-G races during the season. She described those starts as exhilarating, nerve-racking and extremely challenging. Still, the same thought arrived whenever she crossed the finish line. That reaction told Shiffrin she still had something to pursue in the event. She also recognizes how much work remains. Shiffrin said she needs improvement in several clear areas before she can become competitive in super-G. Much of that progress, she believes, will come through repetition and greater exposure to speed. Her brain must relearn how to process the gates, terrain, snow and other demands that arrive at a faster pace. The outcome remains uncertain. Once again, that is part of the attraction. Shiffrin also explained why alpine skiing can remain difficult for casual audiences to understand. Athletes try to recreate the conditions they expect to encounter. However, weather and snow can transform a race. A snowstorm may arrive. Temperatures can rise or fall. Fog can move onto the course between start numbers. Cloud cover can turn a bright track dark within minutes. Shiffrin said those changes can create a difference of five-tenths to a full second. That margin may separate a victory from third, fifth or even 10th place. Many of the variables remain outside an athlete’s control. That unpredictability makes ski racing difficult to explain and forecast. It also ensures that athletes must keep adapting. Even after 16 World Cup seasons, Shiffrin can still encounter something new. Shiffrin’s search for growth extends beyond skiing. During a packed week in New York, she participated in two live recordings of “What’s the Point?” and attended the ESPYS, the TIME100 Sports Gala, Fanatics Fest, sponsor appearances and the FIFA Club World Cup final. Those appearances may look glamorous from the outside. Shiffrin experiences them differently. She described herself as a natural introvert who feels more comfortable behind a helmet and goggles than making small talk on a red carpet. She compared entering a crowded event to walking into a school cafeteria without knowing where to sit. However, those uncomfortable experiences have helped Shiffrin recognize how many people remain unfamiliar with alpine skiing. She views that limited awareness as an opportunity. Her podcast and other projects may help introduce the sport to a broader audience. Her platform also allows her to discuss subjects that matter to her, including grief, post-traumatic stress disorder, mental health, access to sports, cancer research and climate change. Shiffrin recently appeared on Anderson Cooper’s “All There Is” podcast. She said the responses from listeners gave meaning to a conversation that required her to revisit painful experiences. Her skiing created the platform. She does not want to take it for granted. Shiffrin also addressed a persistent misconception about the life of an elite ski racer. After the Olympics, she still had six weeks of racing. Once the season ended, equipment testing followed. June and July then brought an intensive strength and conditioning block. Shiffrin commonly trains twice a day for a combined four to six hours. Media appearances and sponsor commitments fit around those sessions, not in place of them. Her team even considers proximity to a properly equipped gym when selecting lodging. Next comes Southern Hemisphere training before Shiffrin returns to Europe in October for final preparation ahead of the World Cup season. Once racing begins, the circuit moves between countries and occasionally continents until late March. The schedule leaves Shiffrin only four or five weeks a year at her Colorado home. It also limits her concentrated time with fiancé Aleksander Aamodt Kilde, who follows his own training and racing schedule with Norway. Because the women’s and men’s tours usually compete at different venues, the couple receives little uninterrupted time together. Shiffrin said they have not started planning their wedding. The delay does not trouble her. “I know who I want to spend my life with,” she said. For now, they value the limited time they can spend together. Shiffrin has achieved more World Cup success than any alpine ski racer in history. She does not believe that means skiing has nothing left to offer. She wants to learn whether she can reach another level in giant slalom. She wants to discover what greater repetition could unlock in super-G. She also wants to use her platform to bring more attention to alpine skiing and to subjects that matter beyond racing. The records describe what Shiffrin has accomplished. “I simply love skiing,” she said. “And I still feel like there’s more in that.” This article is based on Mikaela Shiffrin’s YouTube video, “Why Do You Keep Going? | My Honest Answer,” published as part of her “What’s the Point?” series. title: BMW F900 GS Adventure: Long-legged tourer, off-road giant, or both? - Yahoo News Canada
content: The rise of adventure bike sales in the UK seems as unstoppable as the rugged, knobby-tyred bikes themselves: latest figures show this segment rising by just over 20 per cent in June 2026, compared to the same month last year. It must be the call of the wild - even when the road runs out, you can keep on riding. In June 2025 2,389 new adventure bikes were registered, rising to 2,871 this year, according to the MCIA (Motorcycle Industry Association). It was a good month all-round; 'modern classics' sales rose just over 23 per cent, 'road sports' by over 22 per cent. By contrast, 'touring' model sales were down nearly 40 per cent. I had plenty of time to ponder this - and wonder whether I was on the 'right' bike - when I spent hours in the saddle of BMW's F900 GS Adventure model, on a 700-mile tour from London to the pretty Gwynedd coast and back. In the heatwave. The ride included hours of boring M4 to reach the Severn Crossing, then beautifully sinuous, undulating roads but, on this trip, no off-road sections which, with its 21-inch front wheel, 230mm of fork and 215 mm rear suspension travel, 230mm of ground clearance, optional Enduro Pro riding mode and off-road swagger, the F900 looked cut out for. Strange, then, that in BMW Motorrad's UK sales blurb, there are no images of the F900 braving deserts, mountains, river crossings; the closest it gets is when it's parked artistically in a summer meadow. Instead, the marketing material stresses the bike's suitability for 'adventure', 'touring', its readiness for 'all short and long trips', even, with the Ride Pro package, its compatibility with 'extensive touring'. Given that BMW has plenty of 'proper' tourers and that it also pitches the bigger, far costlier, heavier R 1300 GS, along with the F900 GS (non-Adventure model) very much as off-road machines, pictured being ridden in rocky streams, desert sand and on forest trails, it's hard to see exactly what kind of riding the F900 is aimed at. Replacing the F850 GS Adventure, the newcomer weighs just two kgs more, has more power (up from 95hp to 105hp), marginally more torque and is claimed to have snappier power delivery. The new bike has beefier, adjustable forks and enduro-style footpegs, perhaps suggesting more aptitude for the rough stuff. More goodies (heated grips, cruise control) now come as standard on the base model. Visually the new bike looks quite different; despite its engine crash bars and sump guard, it appears slightly less off-roady, more tour-y, especially with its 'blocky' panels flanking the tank. So how's it go? The first thing you notice is how heavy it is to heave off the side-stand. Park it carelessly on a camber so that it leans (its stand presents a steep angle anyway) and it can be a struggle getting vertical. It feels tall too, the standard seat height of 875mm leaving me (I measure up at around 5' 10 inches) on tip-toes, not great for tight manoeuvring. (The BMW lower seat option takes it to 825mm, with a further suspension mod taking it down as far as 805mm.) Once rolling, that sensation of top-heavy weight quickly disappears, although it never feels like a lightweight at low speeds. It filters well enough in London traffic however, the lofty seating position giving excellent views over and through traffic, the steering very nice and fluid. The review model came with large, extremely practical, official BMW 'tin' panniers and top box (same key as the huge 23-litre petrol tank, offering tons of space for a week's touring essentials, even if the right-hand-side pannier is slightly tighter to accommodate the high-rise (another nod to off-roading) exhaust. On the M4, the relaxed, low-revving nature of the parallel twin engine was welcome. Some critics say it's an unexciting engine with linear power delivery instead of - presumably more exciting - power 'bands'. I liked it. It pulled beautifully and sonorously from low revs, delivering nice big dollops of torque, vibey character and very usable acceleration for overtaking, even in high gears. It was reasonably comfortable, too, for an hour and a half or so, anyway, before contact points below the hips - and aches in my knees - made stopping for a cuppa enticing. There's an easy-to-operate manual screen that can be adjusted on the fly. With the dash reading 36 degrees I kept the screen down for more cooling and the air felt reasonably 'clean', with little buffeting. On the highest setting my crash helmet was quieter, with less wind rush, slightly less pressure on the chest. The seating 'triangle' - as everyone now calls it - was relaxed; no wrist or arm strain, no backache either. In traffic (possibly because I was activating the clutch lever with just two fingers, making it impossible to pull it all the way in), neutral was sometimes tricky to locate. Only by taking a fistful of clutch, lever right into the bar, could I coax the green light into action; irritating while parking in the burning sun. In Wales, on swooping mountain passes the F900 was highly enjoyable; fun to swing through bends, then open up the throttle to bring the pleasing, relaxing water-cooled motor on-song. I found no issue, on tighter, faster bends, or long sweeping ones, with the 21-inch front wheel. It's a fast enough bike, and the engine is very flexible indeed. The supple ride quality was a thing of beauty. On narrow back-country roads, with grass and gravel creating a loose ridge along the centre of the lanes, the bike remained poised, in its element. It's worth noting that the standard bike comes with traction control and two ride modes; rain and road. Buyers can add the Riding Modes Pro package that includes additional settings (Dynamic, Enduro and Enduro Pro) and that lets you pre-select up to four modes and assign them to a button on the handlebars. Would I have taken it off-road? Not a chance; I like a green lane as much as the next rider but when (not if), it went down, there's no way I could have hoisted the 246kg bike up again, not on my own. This was underlined on-tour twice when, unable to find the 'right' angle in tight mountain pull-in parking spots, my riding companion had to help me push it up off the side stand. I now weigh only 70kgs after recently completing four years of intensive cancer treatment but I'm fairly fit and work out in the gym. I'm not that feeble. A couple of stronger, 'sitter-onners' had the same trouble. So, a highly enjoyable bike on the move but beware if you want to wheel it in and out of a garage or slopey tight spot, if you have short legs or are prone to toppling when parking. I also found it too damn hot. Sure, the effective screen and the see-through 'aerofoils' above and to the side of the tank would be great in rain and winter, and we don't often get 36 degrees (or do we now?). But when the mercury rose, they created a superheated bubble of air from the engine which - when I hit central London after hours boiling up on the M4 - did me in. I think I had mild heat stroke; that's the trouble with layers of biking gear, including airbag 'vest' and long touring boots. I find it a hard bike to categorise. If you just want a tourer, you don't need the height. If you want to go off-road, you won't want that top-heavy tippy feeling - unless you're very good indeed. My guess is that - coming in at just £12,420 for the base F900 GS Adventure (lots more if you want various goodies such as extra riding modes added on), it must be aimed at temping those who can't or won't spend £18,890 on the grander 1300 model. But that bigger bike has tricks up its sleeve including a lower centre of gravity (with that low-down 'boxer' engine) and 'adaptive vehicle height control' that automatically drops the height by 30mm shortly before a stop. If its bigger shaft-drive 1300 brother doesn't appeal however and you swivel back to the chain-drive F900 GSA, it faces very stiff competition from the likes of Triumph's 900 Rally Pro, Suzuki's V-Strom 1050 DE, Honda's Africa Twin, KTM's 890 and a clutch of new Chinese offerings, at substantially less money. Possibly the more practical choice would be the non-Adventure F900 GS, which I've not yet ridden, but which is substantially different from the Adventure model, and has been well received by critics. I wanted to like this bike and did in the bends and to some extent on the m-way. I liked the high build quality and general comfort. But there was always the knowledge that - at some point - I'd have to stop, and plan carefully ahead - or start sweating - just to park and move off again. It's probably one for hard-core, tall, long-legged BMW enthusiasts who don't mind people asking 'why didn't you go for the 1300...' title: How SG.GS is Redefining Global Connectivity with an Execution-Centric Approach - The Fast Mode
content: The connectivity business is changing. On the surface, cross-border enterprise network expansion appears to be surging like never before, as industries become more globalized and workforces, operations, and systems become increasingly distributed. However, the reality is more nuanced: enterprises aren’t looking for simple wholesale access anymore. They are looking for connectivity partners who can move quickly, solve operational challenges in real time, and consistently turn network strategy into tangible business outcomes. An execution-centric approach to building enterprise networks is becoming increasingly popular for modern businesses, who are putting stronger emphasis on being able to deliver reliable connectivity, respond to changes quickly, and scale capacity seamlessly. The largest aspect of this – reliability – concerns the network infrastructure itself. A resilient network often features carrier-grade backbone connectivity, backed by strong SLAs and designed with route diversity, redundant subsea paths, and automated failover. Equally critical is responsiveness – enterprises need partners that can provide immediate, round-the-clock support during network disruptions and changes to ensure operations continue without interruption. A third factor is scale – undoubtedly, one of the most important considerations for fast-growing enterprises. Scale is no longer as simple as maintaining a broad footprint, but having a truly “ubiquitous” network underpinned by flexible capacity and intelligent interconnection, leveraging key capabilities such as elastic bandwidth options, rapid provisioning, dense ecosystem interconnection, and infrastructure capable of supporting new cloud and AI workloads. A fourth and final factor is flexibility. Businesses are increasingly opting for providers who offer customizable architectures, rapid provisioning, and agile models designed to accommodate shifting traffic demands, hybrid cloud environments, and multi-market expansion strategies. For many enterprises, execution ultimately comes down to responsiveness, how quickly providers can provision services, adapt to changing requirements, troubleshoot issues, and support expansion into new markets without adding operational friction. For Asia-headquartered wholesale carrier SG.GS, execution sits at the heart of their commercial expansion strategy. The company provides a suite of connectivity services, spanning IP Transit, Ethernet Private Line, DC Wave, Dedicated Internet Access, Cloud Connect, and IX Peering. They boast a colossal network footprint spanning key Asian cities, including Hong Kong, Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, and Tokyo, as well as several European, U.S., LATAM, and Australian points of presence. However, this scale is just one part of their transformational growth story – a journey that took the company from a simple web hosting platform to a rapidly expanding APAC-headquartered global connectivity provider. According to founder and CTO Heng Chai Tan, the company’s evolution has been driven by a steady commitment to operational delivery, with a focus on three core business tenets – namely agility, customer support, and regional expertise. “Over the last twenty years, we’ve seen immense global growth in connectivity services, a trend that SG.GS has grown alongside in becoming one of the region’s most connected network carriers,” says Tan. Too many providers still compete primarily on footprint and capacity. But enterprise customers today need partners that can execute quickly, adapt to changing requirements and solve operational challenges across markets. This is where we have focused SG.GS – combining regional expertise with engineering-led delivery and long-term customer partnerships. We seek to provide more than just wholesale access to our customers, but a wider strategic partnership centred around their evolving  business and infrastructure requirements. Executing across APAC requires more than footprint alone. Enterprises expanding across the region often face fragmented infrastructure environments, varying regulatory requirements, inconsistent last-mile capabilities, and rapidly shifting capacity demands. SG.GS has positioned itself around helping customers navigate that complexity through regional expertise, engineering-led delivery, and operational responsiveness. That operational model is supported by a network footprint spanning 200+ PoPs across 30+ markets, alongside strategic peering and infrastructure relationships with partners including NTT Communications, Tata Communications, SGIX, HKIX, and BBIX. By helping enterprises navigate local interconnection challenges, infrastructure gaps, and regional deployment complexities SG.GS has established a strong position across both established and emerging growth markets. Execution is ultimately driven by technical competence – but for SG.GS, this is reinforced by an equally strong customer support model. The company works closely with enterprises to design tailored network solutions aligned with specific performance, latency, and scalability requirements, while ensuring customers engage directly with engineers and commercial specialists who understand their markets, regulatory environments, and infrastructure constraints. “Great customer experience is not defined by standardized service delivery and general best practices,” says Ben Cooper, the company’s newly-appointed SVP of Global Network Strategy.“It is defined by the ability to build true partnerships with customers, remain technically responsive to their evolving needs, and design flexible, reliable network solutions that adapt across markets and use cases. Ultimately, it is about delivering networks not just for the customer, but with the customer.” Enterprises are increasingly valuing partners that can consistently translate network strategy into tangible operational outcomes. That focus on operational execution and customer delivery has increasing translated in to commercial momentum and industry recognition, including SG.GS’ double-win at The Fast Mode Awards 2025, which saw the company clinching both the Enterprise Growth Leader and Emerging Telco Brand titles, alongside big names such as Lumen and Indonesia’s Linknet. As enterprise connectivity requirements continue to evolve, SG.GS is positioning itself around a simple premise: growth is not defined by footprint alone, but by the ability to consistently execute for customers across increasingly complex global environments. Through a combination of regional expertise, engineering-led delivery, and customer-focused operational agility, the company continues to build momentum across APAC and key international markets. title: GS Caltex's Socratic AI Trains New Employees via Dialogue - 조선일보
content: The AI adapts questions to guide trainees to solutions, part of the company's DAX initiative AI: “Let me rephrase the question. Do all components in crude oil have the same boiling point?” AI: “Correct. Each component has a different boiling point.” Moments later, the new employee replied, “Ah, so heating separates gasoline and diesel based on their boiling points!” On July 9, at the GS Caltex No. 2 Plant training center in Yeosu, South Jeolla Province, first-year employees Kwon Ji-won and Ko Da-hyeon engaged in a question-and-answer session with an AI instructor on the monitor. Even when the new employees made mistakes, the AI did not immediately provide answers. Instead, it adjusted the difficulty of questions and explanation methods to guide them to the correct answers independently. Once the employees grasped the concept, the AI moved to the next step: “Then, between gasoline and diesel, which one separates first?” The AI teaching the new employees that day was GS Caltex’s self-developed training program, “Socratic AI.” It applies Socrates’ dialectical method—asking continuous questions to lead the other party to find answers independently—to AI. While generative AIs like ChatGPT passively respond to user queries, Socratic AI actively initiates questions and adjusts follow-up questions based on the learner’s responses. AI, which previously served as a “process manager” in manufacturing, has now taken on the role of a “senior mentor” for new employees. The core of Socratic dialogue is “awareness of ignorance.” New engineers often do not even know what they do not know. Chatbot-style AIs that prompt new employees to “ask questions” are often ineffective. Kim Byung-yoon, the company’s education team leader, explained, “This is why GS Caltex focused on this approach.” Socratic AI is not unfamiliar in overseas educational settings. For example, U.S. medical schools actively use AI to engage in dialogues over clinical cases, enhancing trainee doctors’ diagnostic skills. However, businesses have largely overlooked this method, as most corporate AIs are efficiency tools that provide “the fastest answer.” GS Caltex took the counterintuitive approach that “slow AI” is better for nurturing talent. The company’s previous new employee training involved in-house group sessions and one-on-one mentoring by senior on-site staff. Group training struggled to address individual skill gaps, while mentoring required seniors to split their work hours, leading to inconsistent education quality. ◇Beyond Process Optimization: AI That “Nurtures People” To solve this, the Yeosu Plant’s education and digital innovation teams proposed the Socratic AI idea, and Vice Chairman Hur Sae-hong’s approval accelerated development. A team of about 10 veterans—including education specialists, AI developers, and process experts—spent approximately four months developing the system. The key was designing the AI to “endure” knowing the answers. If a learner gave an incorrect response, the AI would simplify the question; if the learner demonstrated sufficient understanding, it would advance to the next stage. This creates personalized learning paths for each trainee. The eight-week pilot program from April this year was successful. Ko Da-hyeon, an employee, said, “New employees hesitate to ask questions, thinking, ‘Is this even worth asking?’ But engaging in dialogues with Socratic AI, which initiates questions first, helped clarify concepts.” Since last year, GS Caltex has pursued DAX (Digital & AI Transformation), combining digital transformation with AI transformation. Socratic AI is part of this initiative. Vice Chairman Hur Sae-hong stated, “The era has arrived where how effectively a company utilizes AI and data determines its sustainable competitiveness,” adding, “Socratic AI is a capable new colleague.” This applies Socrates’ dialectical method—continuously asking questions to lead the other party to find answers independently—to generative AI. While general generative AIs passively respond to user requests, Socratic AI actively initiates questions and continues the dialogue based on the user’s responses.

title: Historic Parity on the Line in GS at Road America - Sportscar365
content: Could Aston Martin, Toyota, become seventh different GS manufacturer to win in seven years at Road America? Road America has emerged as a bit of a wild card round for IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge competitors the last several years. A total of 42 cars are entered for the Road America 120, split 28 GS and 14 TCRs, for the seventh round of the season. Six different manufacturers have won overall and in GS since 2020: McLaren, BMW, Mercedes-AMG, Chevrolet, Porsche and Ford. Of those six, all but Chevrolet are still active. Aston Martin or Toyota could continue the parity streak if either manufacturer wins their first Road America race, and both are coming off highs at Canadian Tire Motorsport Park. Aston Martin won its second straight pole, with Heart of Racing Team’s Hannah Greenemeier following Hannah Grisham as the fastest GS qualifier two weeks earlier at Watkins Glen. Then Toyota won the race in Canada with RAFA Racing’s Kiko Porto and Varun Choksey parlaying their pace into a first victory. The CTMP round shifted the GS title battle to where only 40 points covers the top three. McCumbee McAleer Racing’s Nate Cicero and Robert Noaker now lead by 30 points over Ibiza Farm Motorsport’s Michael Cooper and Moisey Uretsky, with AutoTechnic Racing’s Stevan McAleer and Austin Krainz just ten points further back in third. Tough recent weekends have dropped Turner Motorsport’s Dillon Machavern and Luca Mars and Winward Racing’s Bryce Ward slightly down the order, but still with enough time to claw back the deficit as they’re both within 190 points. TCR saw a new Road America winner last year with Hyundai back on top at the track for the first time since 2020; Bryson Morris and Mark Wilkins delivered the Elantra N TCR’s first win at the venerable 4.048-mile circuit. Morris and Mason Filippi have been the model of consistency in TCR this year, with two wins including last time out at CTMP and five podiums achieved in six races. That sees them 200 points clear of teammates Denis Dupont and Preston Brown. Although that 200-point gap is strong, a tough result for the No. 33 car could bring any of the next five cars into title contention, as they’re only covered by 80 points. Among the handful of changes throughout the grid, Celso Neto is listed alongside Eddie Gou in the No. 55 Gou Racing with Stallion Audi RS 3 LMS TCR. Both Medusa Motorsports and RVA Graphics by Speed Syndicate Motorsports return after at least one-race absences, while LAP Motorsports has entered the No. 6 rather than No. 30 Ford Mustang GT4. This has come after Ford Racing and Multimatic built up a new chassis, which was delivered to the team’s shop in Brownsburg, Ind. on Saturday. Scott Thomson and Clayton Williams will pilot the entry this weekend. Pilot Challenge teams have one practice Thursday, a second Friday morning before qualifying Friday afternoon, and race Saturday at 12:50 p.m. CST. title: Fans Experience Opening Weekend of KAROL G’s Tour - Hudson Valley Press
content:
CHICAGO – Global recording artist KAROL G officially launched her “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” this weekend with two consecutive nights at Soldier Field in Chicago, welcoming more than 90,000 fans throughout the opening weekend. Marking the debut of her largest live production to date, “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” invites audiences into a bold new live experience inspired by the vibrant spirit of Tropicoqueta. More than a concert, opening weekend marked the beginning of a journey that invites audiences around the world to celebrate the music, rhythms and spirit that continue to connect generations across Latin culture. From the opening moments, Soldier Field transformed into a world all its own. Across five acts, the production continuously evolved through immersive staging, live musicians, dynamic choreography and breathtaking visual moments, while pyrotechnics, fireworks and bursts of confetti amplified the energy throughout the night. Complementing the visual experience, KAROL G debuted a series of custom looks created in collaboration with Brett Alan Nelson, ETRO, Michael Schmidt Studios, The Blonds and SEKS, reflecting the bold, fashion-forward identity of the tour. Singer-songwriter Elena Rose opened both sold-out performances as the tour’s special guest, setting the stage for an unforgettable opening weekend. At the heart of the production, the now-signature pool served as one of the show’s defining visual elements, creating unforgettable moments as more than 90,000 fans sang, danced and celebrated together. One of the evening’s most memorable moments came as Academy Award-nominated actor Edward James Olmos appeared on screen to introduce the Tropicoqueta act, setting the stage for mariachi-inspired performances of “Ese Hombre Es Malo,” “200 Copas” and “MAMIII,” creating one of the production’s defining moments. Throughout the night, KAROL G moved effortlessly between reggaetón anthems, intimate ballads and reimagined versions of fan favorites. Fresh cumbia and salsa arrangements of “BICHOTA” and “TUSA” offered new interpretations of two of her biggest hits while keeping the audience on its feet from beginning to end. Opening night concluded with the debut of “MATADORA,” as KAROL G surprised fans with a special closing moment built around the new single, giving the Chicago audience its first introduction to the song before the show came to a close.
Following its sold-out opening weekend in Chicago, the tour continues across North America before traveling through Latin America and Europe, bringing KAROL G’s largest live production to audiences around the world.

title: Mikey G's Feeling at Home in Midtown - The Raincross Gazette
content:
The Elizabeth Street shop is thriving, and its new bagel line, inherited from the bakery it once shared a kitchen with, has customers coming in for reasons beyond the coffee. Four months into its Elizabeth Street location, Mikey G's is among the first food and drink businesses to open since the business corridors inside Magnolia Center started going by Midtown. Mikey G's is not the first business to find success in Magnolia Center. The area has been a vibrant hub of business in Riverside for over half a century. The Sire has endured on Magnolia Avenue for decades, and Condron Coffee and The Outpost are among the wave of successes on Sunnyside Drive. What Mikey G's represents is a continuation, not a beginning. Still, the shop is open and thriving. It opened this spring and has become a go-to for people looking for an excellent product without downtown parking hassles. "This location has really exceeded our expectations," said Jake Driscoll, an owner. "The flow of traffic that has come through, the people who are excited, not only about the drinks, but about the bagels." Driscoll said the Midtown name struck him as a good look for what is happening in Riverside. It is already one of the places people use to explain where Midtown is. That it sits a few blocks from Condron does not seem to trouble him, and neither do the ones opening downtown. A new coffee shop in Riverside has stopped being news and become something closer to a running joke. "There's always going to be more coffee shops that open up, and if that's a reality, we see that as a good thing," Driscoll said. "More coffee in Riverside helps coffee in Riverside as a whole. We're always going to be Mikey G's." Some of the traffic is not there for coffee at all. Mikey G's acquired Parzel's Bagelry, the bakery it once shared a kitchen with at Harvest Christian Fellowship on Arlington, from founder Kali Hathaway, and the bagels have built a following of their own. The bagels that built their own following - Driscoll says some customers come in for these alone, then discover the drinks. (David Fouts) "We owe a lot to Kali," Driscoll said. "She was down to hand off her dream of bagels to us." "We wanted to have a food option, but it seems like we have even a customer base who will come in just to grab a bagel, which is amazing," Driscoll said. "So we have to let them know that we also have delicious drinks as well." They do. The espresso tonics and matcha on tap are worth the trip on a hot afternoon. The original location at Harvest still opens Sundays from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., though the bulk of the business now runs out of Elizabeth Street. What the corridor has is a handful of businesses that opened at different times, for different reasons, and ended up serving the same few blocks. The older ones kept it going through years before the Midtown designation. The newest are opening into a neighborhood that has just been handed a name. "We just get the benefit off of the energy, the momentum that's happening in this side of town," Driscoll said. Driscoll would not say whether more locations are coming. "At the end of the day, we're dreamers," he said. "We're always open to other opportunities, but at this very moment, we're very grateful to be in Midtown." More information: Mikey G's is located at 3780 Elizabeth St. and is open 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily. Business GS E&C completes TBM excavation for Melbourne highway project GS Engineering & Construction announced Tuesday that it has completed tunnel boring machine excavation for a key section of Melbourne's North East Link highway project, marking a major milestone in the South Korean builder's first Australian infrastructure project. Two tunnel boring machines, each measuring 15.6 meters in diameter, reached their designated endpoints after completing their respective excavation sections, the company said.
